standard-vocabulary.text: Anchors publish independently computed signed ledger roots. Ledger providers serve data and proofs, while application services interpret history and build application proofs. A terminal is a lightweight Web2 application with cryptographic capabilities. It checks assets before enabling transaction construction or off-chain data use. Ledger roots cover generic ledger state; application roots cover application state.

terminals-lightweight-web2-applications.text: A terminal is a familiar Web2 application with cryptographic capabilities, suitable for a browser, mobile application or conventional service. Its purpose and risk policy select trusted anchors, required claims, freshness and settlement conditions. The diagram follows that policy to a usable chainpoint, then brings untrusted data and proofs together with signed roots from chosen anchors. Verification enables transaction construction or off-chain data consumption; failed checks block verified use. A report or display needs no transaction submission. Irreversible effects require settlement and authorization. Chain following and heavy data work stay with providers, while ordinary application code and verification libraries implement the terminal. Data and roots may arrive in either order, but their bindings must agree and the data provider cannot choose the terminal’s trust policy.

assets-and-nft-state-outputs.text: An asset identity combines minting policy and asset name. Using it as a unique state identifier requires a policy limiting the asset to one unit and state rules preserving the authoritative output. Inclusion alone proves neither unique supply nor authority. If several candidates are allowed, the application contract must define which is authoritative.

two-roots-with-different-scopes.text: A ledger root covers the indexed ledger quantities at a chainpoint. An application root is inside the state output datum in this integration. Verify the output first, then use its application root to verify the next claim.

ledger-and-application-proofs.text: Ledger proofs support checking existing indexed ledger facts off-chain. Application proofs support application validation and may enter redeemers. Inclusion alone does not prove query completeness or freshness.

transaction-cbor-datums-and-redeemers.text: Transaction CBOR encodes the transaction. Datums carry output-associated application data and redeemers supply script-execution data. Parsing the envelope differs from interpreting Plutus data. The generic service preserves information and applications assign meaning.

chainpoints-views-and-sessions.text: Chainpoints identify positions, views expose state and sessions retain access under a lease. Follow the session page for refusal, retention and rollback behavior.

a-chain-of-application-roots.text: An authenticated application value may carry another root. Every descendant claim requires a checked proof and the expected interpretation. The architecture owns the root-chain diagram and verification order.

untrusted-application-services.text: Application services are untrusted computation providers, just like ledgers. The terminal checks their results against the authenticated application root instead of accepting a service assertion. Follow the trust boundary and delegation story for rejected cases.

follow-the-example.text: Follow the project links into proof composition. CSMT-UTXO supplies the existing engine and measurement starting point. Availability obligations are explained in the market page.
